strengths: Integrating graph-based label propagation and label spreading into classification-based Bayesian optimization is a simple, potentially useful contribution. Supporting both generated unlabeled points and predefined candidate pools gives the approach practical relevance without requiring additional objective evaluations.

The experiments compare against BORE and LFBO with several classifiers and GP-based optimization across synthetic functions, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture search. Twenty repetitions with standard errors provide meaningful evidence of performance gains, particularly on NATS-Bench and several synthetic problems.

The paper clearly acknowledges its foundations in existing density-ratio estimation and semi-supervised learning methods. The appendices provide useful sensitivity studies covering kernel parameters, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling.
weaknesses: The central explanation that semi-supervised learning alleviates overconfidence and improves exploration is insufficiently established. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence through the spatial concentration of high class probabilities, but a broader high-probability region does not itself demonstrate useful exploration. Figures 1 and 8 provide illustrative trajectories rather than quantitative evidence connecting region expansion, escape from local optima, and optimization performance.

The cluster-assumption argument is not justified for the proposed sampling procedure. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points cannot ensure that high-density paths connect points with the same objective-threshold label. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. semi-supervised learning results do not apply to sequential optimization, and it does not establish the asserted decision-region expansion. Consequently, the theoretical discussion provides intuition rather than support for the claimed mechanism.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of unlabeled data. Figure 11 includes a valuable comparison without unlabeled points, but its results are mixed, with the supervised kernel estimator sometimes performing better. That comparison fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn substantially larger values and Figure 10 shows strong sensitivity to beta. Comparisons with appropriately tuned supervised kernel estimators and ablations of the random tie-breaking heuristic are needed to attribute the main gains to semi-supervised propagation.

Important comparison and reproduction details remain unclear. The paper specifies L-BFGS-B with 1,000 starts but does not adequately explain acquisition optimization over discrete pools or for piecewise-constant tree classifiers, nor whether the tie-breaking heuristic is shared with baselines. Input scaling, categorical encoding, and the propagation settings alpha, tolerance, and iteration limit are also unspecified. These choices can materially affect the reported rankings. A random-search baseline would provide an additional useful reference.

The evidence for broader applicability needs qualification. Continuous optimization is evaluated only on four two-dimensional functions. The MNIST experiment uses embeddings from a network trained on 440,000 examples labeled with the same three-digit target, achieving 96.9% test classification accuracy. Although shared embeddings permit comparisons between optimizers, this is a setting with extensive prior target supervision; a baseline ranking candidates using the pretrained classifier would clarify the added value of optimization. Runtime comparisons are also absent: the pool-size timing study uses fixed beta and does not establish the cost of the full adaptive method relative to competitors.

There is a correctable mathematical inconsistency in Section 4.1: the entrywise definition of P normalizes columns and therefore gives P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W. Because Equation 7 subsequently transposes P, the implemented propagation operator needs clarification.
